worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=1$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x+3}-2} & =\frac{1-1}{\sqrt{1+3}-2}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x+3}-2} & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x+3}+2)}{(\sqrt{x+3}-2)(\sqrt{x+3}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x+3}+2)}{{(\sqrt{x+3})}^{2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x+3}+2)}{x+3-4} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x+3}+2)}{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}(\sqrt{x+3}+2) \\  & =\sqrt{1+3}+2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
